After seeing recent news about Donald Trump wanting to reinstate the Glass Stegall Act, I figured there were people who wouldn't know exactly what that was. So, I decided to write up a very quick and dirty explanation.

What is the Glass Stegall Act of 1933?All links are either to Wikipedia or Archive.is

The Glass Stegall act was actually a set of laws detailed out in the larger Banking Act of 1933. In wake of the Great Depression, these laws were put in place to avoid such a financial crisis again.

Glass Stegall was set in place to separate commercial banks from investment banks. In short, if a bank held people's money, they weren't allowed to risk that money in the market on high-risk investing. So, Local Bank, Inc. wasn't allowed to take it's customers deposits and risk it all on 23 Black. The only thing that they could invest on were super low-risk vehicles, such as federal bonds, since they were insured by the government (basically, the government would have to implode for there to be no return on investment).

Joseph E. Stiglitz, economic nobel prize winner, put the intentions of Glass Stegall very well:

Commercial banks are not supposed to be high-risk ventures; they are supposed to manage other peopleâ€™s money very conservatively. It is with this understanding that the government agrees to pick up the tab should they fail. Investment banks, on the other hand, have traditionally managed rich peopleâ€™s money â€” people who can take bigger risks in order to get bigger returns.

Glass Stegall made commercial banks much safer and thus it allowed the government to back them with deposit insurance, thus staving off another Depression.

In 1999, however, Glass Stegall was partially (might as well have been completely) repealed. There was no longer a separation between investment and commercial banking. This is what many to believe was the leading cause of the 2007-08 global financial crisis, (p.s. it was a large factor).

TL;DR: Glass Stegall was a set of provisions laid out in the broader Banking Act of 1933, made in wake of the Great Depression. It's purpose was to separate commercial banking from investment banking. Banks that took people's money for safe keeping weren't allowed to make anything other than super low-risk investments in the market. This stopped banks from essentially "stealing," their customers money by risking it all in the market. In short, it was a separation of banking to allow for safer deposit banking, and to stop another depression.
